subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the radical axis of the circles x² + y² + 4x + 6y − 7 = 0, 4(x² + y²) + 8x + 12y − 9 = 0.

mark_split.label: Write both circles in standard form
Subtract to find the radical axis

insider_note: The second circle is printed with the 4 taken outside a bracket, as 4(x² + y²) — divide the WHOLE equation by 4 (8x, 12y and −9 as well), not just the x² + y² part.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write both circles in standard form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Only the second circle needs dividing here — by 4.
lines: Divide by 4 so x² and y² have coefficient 1:
steps.why: The second circle's leading coefficient of 4 must be divided out of every term, including the constant, before it can be subtracted from S in the radical axis formula.
common_mistakes: Dividing only the 8x + 12y part by 4 and leaving the constant −9 undivided.
Dividing only 4(x² + y²) by 4 and forgetting that every other term (8x, 12y and −9) must also be divided by 4.
steps.memory_tip: A bracket like 4(x² + y²) means the WHOLE equation was scaled by 4 — divide every single term by 4 to undo it, constant included.

steps.label: Subtract to find the radical axis
steps.margin_note: Second mark, for the subtraction and the cleared final line.
steps.why: Subtracting the two standard-form circles cancels x² and y², leaving the radical axis; multiplying through by 4 clears the remaining fraction.
common_mistakes: Computing −7 + 9/4 incorrectly as −7 − 9/4, flipping the sign of the constant.
Stopping at the fractional form 2x + 3y − 19/4 = 0 instead of clearing it to whole numbers.
steps.memory_tip: −7 = −28/4, so −7 + 9/4 = −19/4 — convert to a common denominator before adding, rather than mixing whole numbers and quarters.
